title: Guard this repository's TypeScript against Bun's silent declare strip
description: Bun 1.3.14 strips a top-level binding named declare in a .ts file as if it were a TypeScript ambient declaration: the definition and every bare-identifier call to it vanish with no diagnostic and exit 0. Found while writing WCLI-9's tests, where a helper named declare silently did nothing and the resulting failures pointed at the code under test rather than at the helper. A test helper that silently does not run is worse than one that fails: a security assertion behind it can pass vacuously. Reproduction: a file containing 'function declare(value: string): void { console.log("ran", value); } declare("hello");' prints nothing under bun, prints normally with the same content as .js, and is unaffected when the function is named anything else; 'const declare = () => {}' with 'declare()' behaves the same way, while a member call such as holder.declare() is unaffected. The guard belongs in this repository because its whole test suite is Bun-run TypeScript; the upstream report is the operator's to route.

acceptanceCriteria.text: A repository check fails, with the offending file and line named, when any tracked .ts file declares a top-level binding named declare or calls it as a bare identifier
The guard is proven both ways: it reports a deliberate case in a test fixture, and it passes on the current tree
The check runs as part of bun run check rather than as a separate command nobody runs

plan: 1. Verify the premise first-hand and find the exact signatures: top-level and nested definitions both vanish, the const form vanishes, a member call and an ambient declaration do not.
2. Write scripts/check-reserved-bindings.mjs: scan the tracked .ts files, mask comments and string contents so prose cannot trip it, and name file and line for a definition or a bare call.
3. Wire it into bun run check, and prove it both ways in a test - a deliberate fixture it reports, the current tree it passes, plus the near-misses it must not report.
implementationNotes:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-29, in this pull request.

PREMISE VERIFIED FIRST-HAND before the guard was written, four ways on bun 1.3.14, because a gate built on an unverified premise is the defect this task is about:
- a `function declare` plus a bare `declare("hello")` in a .ts file prints NOTHING and exits 0;
- the same file with the name changed prints, and the same content as .js prints, so it is the bare name in a TypeScript file that is stripped rather than the name itself;
- `const declare = (value) => { ... }` with `declare("hello")` prints NOTHING;
- `holder.declare("hello")` prints, and `declare const something: number` works, so neither a member call nor the legitimate ambient keyword is affected.
ONE CORRECTION TO THE REPORT: a `function declare` nested inside another function is stripped too, so this was never only a top-level hazard. The guard therefore scans at any indentation, which is strictly wider than the criterion and cannot produce a false positive, because `declare` is a keyword and no binding is ever legitimately named it.

WHAT THE GUARD IS. scripts/check-reserved-bindings.mjs reads the tracked .ts files (git ls-files, so a staged file is covered and an untracked scratch file is not its business) and reports, with file and line: a definition named declare (function, const, let, var, class, at any indentation, plus an import binding) and a bare call declare(...). Comments and the contents of strings and template literals are masked before matching, so prose or a test's expected-output literal cannot trip it, and the legitimate ambient forms - declare const x, declare function f, declare module - are explicitly not reports. One measured limit is recorded in its header rather than hidden: a call inside a template interpolation is masked with the template and not seen, though the definition that call needs would still be reported.

PROVEN BOTH WAYS, and at the level that matters rather than only in unit terms:
- test/reserved-bindings.test.ts pins four hazards (definition, nested definition, import binding, a call with no definition) and six near-misses (the ambient keyword, a member call, an object property, a comment, a string, a template), plus the clean tree with the count it read - a check that read nothing and one that read everything and found nothing otherwise print the same thing (ADR 0008).
- END TO END, measured rather than inferred: a hazard staged as test/support/hazard-probe.ts made `bun run reserved:check` exit 1 naming test/support/hazard-probe.ts:1 and :4; removing the file returned it to exit 0. The probe is not in this commit.

AC3: wired into `bun run check` as reserved:check, and the run says so - "reserved binding check: 89 file(s), 0 bindings named declare" - so it is not a command nobody runs. Suite: 678 pass, 0 fail, the 3 pre-existing lint warnings, layer check 0 violations.

A .quest note for WCLI-46 rides in this pull request: the routing correction for the sweep question, which is a tracker change rather than part of this task.
